Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

In Florida, a home insured by Citizens Property Insurance with wind coverage must also carry flood insurance. In a high-risk zone (A or V) this has applied since 2023 (new policies from April 1, renewals from July 1), whatever the home is worth. Outside those zones it phases in by rebuilding cost: from January 1, 2026 at $400,000 or more, and from January 1, 2027 for all other Citizens homes. Condo-unit and no-wind policies are exempt.

85.4% of Lee County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 85.4% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 48,496 NFIP flood claims and $4.0 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2022, 2024 and 2017.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2022 ($3,385,377,866), 2024 ($419,597,083), 2017 ($65,890,296). Total paid $3,950,590,715: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 48,496 claims since 1978 against 134,473 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for 45.7% of the 33,607 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 33,607 policies reporting one)45.7%Florida: 38.6%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)83.7%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 34,610 claims paid with a damage figure)6.6%

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one; many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

75.5% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $1,344, full-risk $3,461 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$1,344
  • Median full-risk premium$3,461
  • Pay below full-risk75.5% of 53,965Florida: 49.8%

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for river flooding and Very High for coastal flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskVery High
  • Inland flood riskRelatively High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. A place with many valuable buildings can have a large total loss and a low loss per dollar, so the rating and the percentile below can differ. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $13.8 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 80% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $95.2 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 33% of U.S. counties. Any loss figure is a whole-county model estimate of all flood loss, insured or not, averaged per year, so it runs far above the insurance payouts shown elsewhere on this page; it is never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 5,179 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 153 records are from homes on FEMA's severe repetitive loss list.

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid records since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $504.1 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,001 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the download's own record total.

In-force count: 134,473 policy units (from 90,224 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA's official count for July 31, 2026 was 132,012: a 1.9% difference. Download check: policies: 90,224 of 90,224 fetched; claims: 48,496 of 48,496 fetched.
